passage: Darshan here. I run the stall next to Anusha's at the weekend market, so I heard the whole thing. Farhan, an adviser from the city, told Anusha, "Double your price on the handmade candles. Premium sells." Anusha wrote it down and nodded at every line. I did not hear a single "why". The next Saturday, candles that sold at forty went up to eighty. Nobody bought. Farhan's customers in the city pay for the box and the fancy label; ours are neighbours who compare with the shop by the bus stand. By afternoon Anusha's table was still full and she was rearranging it for the third time. I don't know if Anusha blamed the advice or the customers. She only said, "He's the expert."

qa.q: What did Farhan tell Anusha to do?
qa.a: Farhan told Anusha to double the price on the handmade candles.

qa.q: How might Anusha have felt as the candles did not sell?
qa.a: Anusha probably felt worried and uncertain, but covered it by saying "He's the expert."

qa.q: What could Anusha have asked Farhan before changing the price?
qa.a: Anusha could have asked why he suggested it and whether it works in a small weekend market like hers, or tried the new price on only some candles.

qa.q: How might customers at the market see the doubled price?
qa.a: Customers might compare it with the shop by the bus stand and think it too much for a market stall.

grounding: Shows an entrepreneur following an adviser's pricing tip without asking why, missing that the adviser's market differs from hers.

Week 1: At the start-up meet, Irfan, a mentor who advises café owners in the big city, looked at Aparna's price list for her home-baked cakes. "Too cheap," he said. "Double everything. People pay for premium." Aparna nodded and wrote it down. She didn't ask why.

Week 3: She printed new cards with the doubled prices. Her regulars in the small town, mostly teachers and shop owners ordering for birthdays, went quiet. Only two orders came that week instead of the usual nine.

Week 5: A neighbour said gently, "Beta, we loved your cakes, but this is city money." Aparna sat with the order book and realised Irfan's clients were office crowds in the city, not her street. She had never asked what his advice was based on.

qa.q: How many orders came in week 3, compared with usual?
qa.a: Only two orders instead of the usual nine.

qa.q: How did Aparna feel when she sat with the order book in week 5?
qa.a: She probably felt dismayed and a bit foolish, realising she had followed Irfan's advice without asking what it was based on.

qa.q: What could Aparna have asked Irfan in week 1?
qa.a: She could have asked why he suggested doubling, and who his clients were, then tested one new price with a few regulars before changing everything.

qa.q: How did the change look to Aparna's regular customers?
qa.a: To her regulars it felt like the cakes were suddenly priced for the city, not for them, so they quietly stopped ordering.

grounding: A young entrepreneur follows an adviser's pricing tip without asking why and misses that his market differs from hers.

passage: Let me tell you something from when I was twenty-five, before this workshop had a sign board. I made hand-stitched cushion covers, and I found an adviser, Francis, who had helped big wholesale sellers. He said, "Cut your price in half. Win on volume." He sounded so sure, and I was so eager, I didn't ask a single question. I cut my prices. But my buyers were small boutiques. They saw the new price and thought the quality had dropped. Two stopped ordering. One owner told me, "At that price, it can't be handwork." Francis wasn't wrong for his world. His world was different from mine. Remember that, when you start: Binita Aunty learnt it the costly way.

qa.q: What did Francis tell young Binita to do?
qa.a: "Cut your price in half. Win on volume."

qa.q: Why didn't young Binita question Francis's advice?
qa.a: She was eager and he sounded so sure, so she felt too impressed and hurried to ask why.

qa.q: At what point in the story could Binita have made a better choice?
qa.a: When Francis gave the advice; asking what kind of sellers he had helped would have shown his wholesale world differed from her boutique buyers.

qa.q: How did the boutique owners see the lower prices?
qa.a: They took the cheaper price as a sign the quality had dropped, and one said it couldn't be handwork at that price.

grounding: An elder recalls following an adviser's pricing advice without asking why and missing that his market differed from hers.
